question: A 28-year-old man suffers a spinal cord injury after a road traffic accident. During examination, it is noted that he has involuntary, unannounced urination. There is no evidence of urinary tract infection, and he reports loss of bladder control since the injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: After a spinal cord injury, the bladder function evolves: Spinal shock phase (initially): Atonic, Autonomous Bladder (overflow incontinence). Recovery phase (weeks-months later): If the injury is above the sacral micturition center (S2-S4), the micturition reflex can become hyper-reflexive and spastic. The bladder empties suddenly and involuntarily when filled to a certain volume, without the patient's awareness. This condition is called an Automatic Bladder (or hyperreflexic/spastic neurogenic bladder).

question: A boy presented in ER after RTA with hemi section of cord. On examination which sensation will be spared on the ipsilateral side below the level of lesion.
explanation: This is a case Brown-SÃ©quard syndrome resulting from the hemicord lesion. The pathway for Tickle (Spinothalamic tract) crosses immediately in the spinal cord, so the fibers for the ipsilateral side are already on the intact, opposite side of the cord. Conversely, the pathways for Two-point discrimination, Vibration, and Proprioception (Dorsal Columns) ascend ipsilaterally and are therefore lost on the side of the lesion.

explanation: Brown-SÃ©quard Syndrome results from a spinal cord hemisection (damage to one lateral half of the cord). It causes ipsilateral paralysis (motor loss on the same side as the lesion) and ipsilateral loss of proprioception/vibration (damage to the Dorsal Columns). Crucially, it causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (due to damage to the Spinothalamic Tract after it has crossed).
